note: Recipes for doing real ML with no GPU. Times are rough orders of magnitude on a modern 4–8 core laptop CPU unless stated — treat them as 'minutes / hours / overnight', not as benchmarks. Nothing here is a substitute for running it yourself.

tiers.name: Laptop CPU only
tiers.spec: 4–8 cores, 8–16 GB RAM, no discrete GPU
tiers.fits: Models under ~150M params if you're patient. NumPy/PyTorch CPU, tiny transformers, tabular models, classical ML, tokenizer training, distillation of tiny students.
tiers.watch: Set torch.set_num_threads() to your physical core count, keep batch size small, and use fp32 (bf16 on CPU is often slower).

tiers.name: Google Colab free tier
tiers.spec: One T4 16 GB (sometimes P100), ~3–6h sessions, idle timeout
tiers.fits: LoRA/QLoRA on 7B–13B models, small diffusion models, anything that needs a GPU for under a few hours.
tiers.watch: Sessions die. Checkpoint to Google Drive every N steps or you will lose work. Save optimizer state, not just weights.

tiers.name: Kaggle notebooks
tiers.spec: 30 GPU-hours/week (P100 or T4 x2), 20h internet off, 9h with internet
tiers.fits: The best free GPU allowance that exists. Multi-day experiment schedules if you split them into weekly chunks.
tiers.watch: Internet is off by default — upload datasets as Kaggle Datasets first.

tiers.name: Used consumer GPU
tiers.fits: 12–16 GB VRAM runs 7B QLoRA, Stable Diffusion inference + light training, and every recipe below comfortably.
tiers.watch: VRAM is the only number that matters. 12 GB beats 8 GB for everything you'll do.

recipes.title: Grokking on modular addition
recipes.tagline: Watch a network memorise, then suddenly generalise — the cleanest demo in ML.
recipes.time: 10–40 min for a small run; the classic paper-scale run is hours
recipes.why: The model is a ~15M-param transformer on a 2-digit addition task. The dataset is tiny, so it fits in RAM and the compute is dominated by small matmuls — a CPU handles it fine, just slowly.
learn: weight decay as a generalisation trigger
why 'converged' is not the same as 'done'
recipes.code:
pip install torch numpy matplotlib
python train.py --p 97 --epochs 40000 --wd 1.0   # grok
python train.py --p 97 --epochs 40000 --wd 0.0   # no grok
recipes.gotcha: The interesting thing happens 10–100x after train accuracy hits 100%. If you stop at convergence you see nothing. Log val accuracy every 100 steps for the whole run.

recipes.title: Train a 10M-param GPT from scratch
recipes.tagline: A real language model, character-level, on your laptop.
recipes.why: nanoGPT at ~10M params on TinyShakespeare (1 MB of text) converges to recognisable Shakespearean English on a CPU. The code is ~300 lines and readable end to end.
recipes.code:
git clone https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT
python data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py
python train.py config/train_shakespeare_char.py --device=cpu --compile=False
recipes.gotcha: Set --compile=False on CPU. torch.compile is a GPU win and a CPU waste.

recipes.title: Train your own BPE tokenizer
recipes.tagline: The one part of the LLM stack you can rebuild completely from scratch in an afternoon.
recipes.why: BPE training is a counting problem. 50k merges over a 1 GB corpus runs on CPU; over a 10 MB corpus it takes seconds.
recipes.code:
pip install tokenizers
python -c "from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, trainers, pre_tokenizers; \
t=Tokenizer(models.BPE(unk_token='<unk>')); t.pre_tokenizer=pre_tokenizers.Whitespace(); \
t.train(['corpus.txt'], trainers.BpeTrainer(vocab_size=30000, special_tokens=['<unk>','<s>','</s>'])); \
t.save('tok.json')"
recipes.gotcha: Then open this page's Tokenizer tab and compare your tokenizer against the big ones on the same Hindi paragraph. That comparison is the whole lesson.

recipes.title: LoRA fine-tune a 0.5B model on CPU
recipes.tagline: Real fine-tuning, no GPU, if you pick a small enough base model.
recipes.time: 1–4 hours for a few thousand examples
recipes.why: A 0.5B model in fp32 is ~2 GB. With LoRA you only backprop through a few hundred thousand trainable params, so the compute is dominated by the frozen forward pass — slow but finite.
learn: why rank matters less than data quality
recipes.code:
pip install transformers peft datasets accelerate
# base: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, r=8, target q_proj,v_proj, 3 epochs
# ~2–5 examples/sec on 8 cores
recipes.gotcha: For 7B+ models this is a Colab/Kaggle job, not a CPU job. QLoRA specifically needs a CUDA GPU for the 4-bit kernels.

recipes.title: Distil a tiny student from a big teacher
recipes.tagline: Steal a big model's behaviour into something that runs on a phone.
recipes.why: The teacher only runs inference (or you can pre-generate its outputs once), and the student is tiny. Pre-generating teacher outputs to disk turns the whole job into a normal supervised training run.
learn: why the student beats its own hard-label training
recipes.code:
# 1. run teacher once, save (input, logits) pairs
# 2. train student with KL(teacher_logits/T, student_logits/T) * T^2 + CE(labels)
recipes.gotcha: Cache the teacher outputs. Re-running the teacher every epoch is the difference between an hour and a day.

links.label: Hinton et al., Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network

recipes.title: Tiny diffusion model on MNIST
recipes.tagline: DDPM small enough that you can read every line of it.
recipes.why: A small U-Net on 28x28 is maybe 2M params. The noise schedule and loss are ~50 lines. CIFAR-10 also works but wants hours.
learn: why you predict noise not images
recipes.code:
pip install torch torchvision matplotlib
# ~2M param U-Net, 1000 timesteps, cosine schedule, EMA on weights
recipes.gotcha: Use EMA of the weights for sampling. Without it your samples look noticeably worse and you'll blame the wrong thing.

recipes.title: Backprop from scratch in NumPy
recipes.tagline: Two hours that make every framework feel transparent forever after.
recipes.time: 2 hours of your life, seconds of compute
recipes.why: No GPU is involved anywhere in autograd. You write the forward pass, derive the gradients by hand, and check them against numerical differentiation.
learn: what a framework is actually doing for you
recipes.code:
# gradient check: (f(w+eps) - f(w-eps)) / (2*eps) should match your analytic grad
# if rel error > 1e-5, your gradient is wrong — the network will still 'train', just worse
recipes.gotcha: Always gradient-check. A subtly wrong gradient trains, just slowly, and you will waste a week debugging your 'architecture'.

recipes.title: Beat a neural net with gradient boosting
recipes.tagline: On tabular data this is true more often than people admit.
recipes.why: LightGBM and XGBoost are CPU-native, multithreaded, and extremely strong on structured data. This is where a laptop is genuinely competitive with a cluster.
learn: when a transformer is the wrong tool
recipes.code:
pip install lightgbm scikit-learn pandas
# always set early_stopping_rounds and use out-of-fold predictions for ensembling
recipes.gotcha: Your leakage is almost always in the preprocessing. Fit the scaler/imputer inside the CV fold, never on the full dataset.

links.label: Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?

recipes.title: DQN on CartPole / LunarLander
recipes.tagline: Reinforcement learning that finishes before your coffee gets cold.
recipes.why: The environments are 2–8 dimensional and the policy network is 2 hidden layers of 64 units. RL here is CPU-bound on environment stepping, not GPU-bound.
recipes.code:
pip install gymnasium stable-baselines3
python -c "import gymnasium, stable_baselines3 as sb3; \
m=sb3.DQN('MlpPolicy','CartPole-v1',verbose=1).learn(50000)"
recipes.gotcha: Run 5 seeds and plot all of them. Single-seed RL results are noise.

recipes.title: Fine-tune sentence embeddings
recipes.tagline: The highest-ROI ML task that fits on a laptop.
recipes.why: A 110M-param encoder with contrastive loss on a few thousand pairs beats a general-purpose embedding model on your specific retrieval task most of the time.
learn: why cosine similarity is a choice not a law
recipes.code:
pip install sentence-transformers datasets
# MultipleNegativesRankingLoss + in-batch negatives, 1–3 epochs
recipes.gotcha: Evaluate on retrieval metrics, not loss. Loss going down and recall@10 staying flat is completely normal.

recipes.title: Free-GPU session discipline
recipes.tagline: The actual skill that makes free GPUs usable.
recipes.why: Free tiers kill your session on an idle timer, on a usage cap, and sometimes for no reason. Your code has to assume death at any moment.
learn: how to read a training curve
recipes.code:
# every N steps, to Google Drive:
#   model.pt, optim.pt, scheduler.pt, epoch, rng state, best metric
# on start: resume if the checkpoint exists
# log to a CSV in Drive, not just stdout — the notebook dies, the Drive file doesn't
recipes.gotcha: Save the RNG state. Without it, resumed runs silently diverge and you'll draw wrong conclusions from your ablations.

recipes.title: Build an eval set before you build a model
recipes.tagline: Zero compute, biggest leverage of anything on this page.
recipes.why: 50–200 hand-written examples with known-good answers tell you more about your model than any leaderboard, and they cost nothing to run.
learn: why a metric you can't compute is not a metric
recipes.code:
# examples.jsonl: {"input": ..., "expected": ..., "category": ...}
# report accuracy per category, not just overall — the overall number hides everything
recipes.gotcha: Keep a hidden holdout you never look at while iterating. The moment you tune against your eval set, it stops being an eval set.
